extracted.intended_audience: graduate students and researchers in geometric analysis / differential geometry studying Perelman's Ricci flow with surgery
extracted.subtask_description: Analysis of three-dimensional Ricci flow solutions with δ-cutoff surgeries: hypotheses (volume, curvature lower bounds, cutoff radii) that guarantee local curvature estimates, canonical neighborhood properties, and long-time asymptotics via rescaling limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Curvature control from local volume and lower curvature bound (Theorem 7.5.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given ε>0 and w>0 there exist τ=τ(w,ε)>0, r̄= r̄(w,ε)>0, θ=θ(w,ε)>0, T=T(w,ε)>0 and K=K(w,ε)<∞ with the following property: suppose a solution constructed by Theorem 7.4.3 (Ricci flow with surgery, normalized compact orientable 3-manifold, nonincreasing r(t)) is defined on [0,t0] with each δ-cutoff at time t in [0,t0] satisfying δ(t) ≤ r̄√t0 and t0 ≥ T. Let r0 satisfy θ^{-1} h ≤ r0 ≤ r̄√t0 (h is the maximal cutoff radius for surgeries in [t0/2,t0], h=0 if no surgery), and assume on Bt0(x0,r0) at time t0 we have Rm(x,t0) ≥ - r0^{-2} and Vol_{t0}(Bt0(x0,r0)) ≥ w r0^3. Then the solution is well-defined on the parabolic neighborhood P(x0,t0,r0/4, τ r0^2] and satisfies R(x,t) < K r0^{-2} there.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constants τ, r̄, θ, T, K depend only on w and ε. The hypotheses combine a local lower curvature bound, a local noncollapsing/volume lower bound, and a restriction relating r0 to the maximal surgery cutoff radius and the global time scale r̄√t0. The statement is used to exclude high curvature blow-up in the specified parabolic region. If r0 violates the relation to r̄√t0 or the volume lower bound fails, the conclusion may not hold. The proof uses canonical neighborhood arguments, pinching assumptions, and standard volume comparison/Bishop–Gromov.

rubrics_metrics.name: Canonical neighborhood property for high scalar curvature points
rubrics_metrics.description: Points with sufficiently large scalar curvature (above specified thresholds depending on chosen constants like ¯Q, K1, etc.) satisfy the canonical neighborhood statement: their neighborhoods are either strong ε-necks, ε-caps, or modeled on pieces of ancient κ-solutions, and they enjoy gradient and curvature derivative estimates as in the canonical neighborhood assumption.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text constructs an adjusted point (¯x,¯t) by an induction so that it fails the canonical neighborhood statement, rescales at that point, and derives contradictions by obtaining an ancient κ-solution. Thus the canonical neighborhood statement is validated (statements (i)-(iii)). The canonical neighborhoods are 'strong' (ε-necks are strong), and pinching, gradient estimates, and surgery design (cutoff thresholds) are crucial. Numeric constants (e.g. factors like 1/20 η^{-1}, K1, ¯Q) appear in the neighborhood scale/thresholds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice and monotonicity of surgery cutoff parameter δ(t)
rubrics_metrics.description: For each fixed A one can define ¯δ_A(t0) and then adjust ¯δ_A(t0) so that it is nonincreasing in t0; in applications one may redefine δ(t) (and take δ(t) ≤ ¯δ(t) where ¯δ(t) tends to zero as t→∞).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The surgery parameter δ(t) must be chosen small enough (depending on local constants like A and time) so that the canonical neighborhood statements and curvature estimates hold. One may take δ(t) ≤ min(1/(2 e^2 log(1+t)), δ0, ¯δ2(t+1)(2t)) so that δ(t) → 0 as t → ∞. Design of cutoff surgeries ensures surgeries only occur on δ-necks and scalar curvature at surgery points is at least (¯δαβ)^{-2} in rescalings used in the proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lower bound evolution for minimum scalar curvature R_min(t)
rubrics_metrics.description: For solutions with surgeries (surgeries occur only on δ-necks and do not affect where R_min(t) is achieved), R_min(t) satisfies d/dt R_min(t) ≥ (2/3) R_min(t)^2 for t in surgery-free intervals, and hence after normalization R_min(t) ≥ - (3/2) / (t + 3/2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because surgeries remove components with nonnegative scalar curvature and are performed only on δ-necks, they do not increase the minimum negative scalar curvature. This differential inequality provides a uniform-in-time lower bound for R_min(t), used in volume evolution estimates and long-time behavior analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monotonicity and control of scaled volume V(t)(t + 3/2)^{-3/2}
rubrics_metrics.description: The quantity V(t)·(t + 3/2)^{-3/2} is nonincreasing in time along Ricci flow with surgeries, and one has the differential inequality d/dt log V(t) ≤ 3/(2(t + 3/2)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because surgeries do not increase volume and by using the evolution equation dV/dt = -∫ R dV together with the lower bound for R_min(t), one obtains monotonicity of the scaled volume. This monotonicity is used to control total volume at large times and to extract integral control terms (see (7.6.4)) that feed into asymptotic arguments and rescaling limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rescaled parabolic-limit criterion for constant sectional curvature (Lemma 7.6.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: If for a sequence of times t_α → ∞ and points x_α the rescalings of the solution on parabolic neighborhoods P(x_α, t_α, r√t_α, r^2 t_α) with factor t_α^{-1} (shifting times so t_α → 1) converge in C^∞ to a smooth limiting solution defined on P(¯x,1,r,1/4), then the limiting solution has constant sectional curvature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This lemma provides the criterion: convergence of appropriately rescaled parabolic neighborhoods (with the given time and spatial scaling) to a smooth limit implies the limit is a constant-curvature metric. It is used to deduce asymptotic roundness or hyperbolicity in blow-down/large-time limits. The assumption requires uniform curvature and noncollapsing controls on the rescaled neighborhoods to pass to the limit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local curvature control from noncollapsing and volume (Lemma 7.6.2(i))
rubrics_metrics.description: Given ε>0, and given w>0, r>0, ξ>0, there exists T = T(w,r,ξ,ε) such that if at time t0 ≥ T the geodesic ball Bt0(x0, r√t0) has volume at least w r^3 t0^{3/2} (equivalently a uniform lower bound proportional to (r√t0)^3) and appropriate local pinching/lower-curvature hypotheses hold, then the curvature at x0 at time t0 satisfies |2t R_ij + g_ij| < ξ (in particular the curvature is small at that scale).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The proof reduces to applying Theorem 7.5.2 on a smaller radius r0 = min(r, r̄) and then taking rescalings t0^{-1} as t0 → ∞; the constants depend on w and ε. One obtains an estimate of the form |Rm| ≤ K'(r0√t0)^{-2} on a parabolic neighborhood, which yields the smallness of the scaled Ricci tensor combination. The argument uses volume comparison, pinching, and compactness arguments to take limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extension of the local curvature control to larger spatial scales (Lemma 7.6.2(ii))
rubrics_metrics.description: Given additionally an A < ∞, the smallness estimate (|2t R_ij + g_ij| < ξ) can be ensured for all points in Bt0(x0, A r√t0) (a larger ball) by taking T depending on A in addition to the other parameters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To extend the estimate from the central ball to a larger ball one needs uniform scalar curvature upper bounds on a larger parabolic neighborhood; the text employs Theorem 7.5.1(ii) (canonical neighborhood control) and pinching to get these bounds. Care is needed because the local radius r0 used in Theorem 7.5.2 may be much larger than the universal ¯r(A,ε) when A is large; the argument overcomes this by a covering/iteration technique and application of prior curvature and volume estimates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forward parabolic neighborhood curvature control (Lemma 7.6.2(iii))
rubrics_metrics.description: The same smallness estimate can be propagated to the forward parabolic neighborhood P(x0,t0, A r√t0, A r^2 t0): that is, the bound holds for all (x,t) with x in Bt(x0, A r√t0) and t in [t0, t0 + A r^2 t0].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This extends spatial control to a space-time region forward in time. The proof uses the Li–Yau–Hamilton inequality, gradient estimates from canonical neighborhoods, and previous curvature bounds to ensure the rescaling limits agree and that no surgeries or blow-ups occur in that forward neighborhood. Constants again depend on A, w, r, ε.
